html:
The refounding of the Greek town of Byzantium on the Bosporus as a new Roman capital by Constantine the Great, dedicated on 11 May 330. He called it New Rome, but it soon took his name: Constantinople, "Constantine's city".

The site was superb. It sat on a peninsula where Europe meets Asia, on the strait between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, easy to defend by sea and close to the threatened Danube and Persian frontiers. Constantine filled it with a palace, a hippodrome, a senate house, churches, statues taken from across the empire, and the Column of Constantine in his forum. Its citizens got free bread, as in Rome.

It grew into the largest and richest city in Europe for much of the Middle Ages, capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire. Theodosius II gave it the Theodosian Walls, and Justinian the Hagia Sophia. It held out until the Ottoman conquest of 1453, and as Istanbul it became the Ottoman capital.
